cmyk-ux/r4y: R4Y is a Rust-based experimental Windows compatibility runtime for Xbox Series X|S / Scarlett software. It combines native x64 title execution, selected KernelX and XGameRuntime HLE, a D3D12.X-to-host-D3D12 backend, and GFX10/RDNA2 shader translation to DXIL.

The investigation produced several concrete engineering results, including a Wave64-to-Wave32 shader path exercised on a physical RTX 3070, real title pipelines that were previously rejected and later successfully created, D3D12 descriptor/command-list fixes, and a safer indirect-argument clamp design.

It did **not** produce a playable or generally compatible runtime. The investigated title still encounters GPU-progress failure / D3D12 device-hung behavior. The exact dispatch or synchronization condition responsible has not been isolated, descriptor virtualization is incomplete, and some shader patterns remain intentionally unsupported.
- **Observed:** present in a user-provided runtime log or crash report, without a proven causal explanation.
Dates and commit references are included because later code, cache state, title builds, drivers, or host adapters can change the result.

The implementation queries the host's supported wave-lane range, passes it into shader translation, refuses fixed wave sizes that the adapter cannot execute, and includes the host wave range in the shader-cache fingerprint. This avoids reusing a shader translation produced for a different wave capability.

2. **Bounded console-flow fallback:** for eligible programs containing cross-half operations, the translator can retry with console-wave control flow for exactly one console Wave64 group per thread group (at most 64 threads). It preserves per-instruction EXEC guards, makes both host halves follow the same console-wave branch decisions, and exchanges selected cross-half values/masks through two group-shared dwords with barriers.

The RTX 3070 test completed with **1 passed, 0 failed** and explicitly reported that the split path was active. The successful test covered lane order for 32/64/128-thread cases, DPP row masks, VCC ballot/count, MBCNT, cross-half v_readlane and v_writelane, v_readfirstlane, SAVEEXEC/SCC behavior, a branch with one half inactive, and a divergent loop that reads a lane in the other half. Earlier failed assertions were traced to incorrect VOP1 source encodings in the test fixtures; those fixture wo

**Real-title evidence:** on a correctly rebuilt Diagnostics runtime, the RTX 3070 reported lanes_min=32 lanes_max=32. Two compute shaders previously rejected for requiring Wave64 — 88994c3496045f51 and 13dfdd3b1136e407 — were freshly translated, had host pipelines created, and later reached first bind. The corresponding earlier run had logged 136 host-pipeline refusals and 168 “Shader wants wave lane count of 64” messages. This is meaningful progress for those two pipelines, not proof that all t
- A later command list reported approximately **8,155 ms** for 26 commands; the associated submission was approximately **8.199 seconds across 33 lists**.
- D3D12 reported DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG (0x887A0006), describing a TDR after commands took an unreasonable time to execute.
- DRED breadcrumbs stopped around a dispatch, but the old output did not conclusively identify whether the relevant list belonged to a main command list or an internal prelude.

The 3.09-second dispatch is a strong lead, but it has **not** been proven to be the dispatch that caused the later device removal. Most per-command values in the later slow list were displayed as 0.0 ms; this is not evidence that those commands consumed no GPU time.

A separate title-side report showed an access violation (0xc0000005) writing to address zero at title-image offset +0x23cf683. Research in [XCL issue #505](https://github.com/xcl-dev/xcl/issues/505) identifies the same offset in the target title as an intentional GPU-progress watchdog path: when the title does not observe expected GPU progress, it deliberately writes to null. This supports interpreting the title exception as a watchdog symptom, not automatically as a random R4Y null-pointer defe

Memory/pool counters were high in the same general period, so memory pressure remains a secondary lead. The evidence does not establish OOM as the cause. Keep the title watchdog, D3D12 TDR, and any actual allocator failure as distinct failure classes.

PR #16 adds instrumentation to associate DRED breadcrumbs with both the main command list and R4Y's internal prelude lists, and adds depth-twin converter dispatch markers. These changes are diagnostic instrumentation; a post-change RTX 3070 run is still needed.
### 3. NVIDIA's logical descriptor heap exceeds the physical host limit — confirmed limitation, not solved

In the captured RTX 3070 run, the title requested **1,245,184** shader-visible view descriptors while the host D3D12 adapter accepted **1,000,000**. One observed fallback layout partitioned the host heap into:

The current capped-heap fallback prevents out-of-bounds host writes and avoids some transient/persistent aliasing. It is **not complete descriptor virtualization**. Title descriptors above the mirrored prefix are not preserved as ordinary title descriptors; some shader-side indices are clamped to safe null entries. Logs showed accesses/touches to high logical indices, often with for_draw=false, which does not prove that every such descriptor was consumed by a draw.

A correct solution must consistently map logical title indices to physical host slots, preserve high descriptors, keep dynamic root-view and fresh-table allocations valid, handle raw descriptor copies into title heaps, and make generated shader indexing use the same mapping. Simply increasing the mirrored count would exceed the physical host limit or collide with internal allocations. Suppressing the warning is not a fix.
Tracking issue: [R4Y #4 — Virtualize title descriptor indices](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/issues/4), still open at this snapshot.

A separate GPU-Based Validation report found pixel shaders expecting a Texture2D SRV while host view-heap slot zero contained a Texture1D SRV. Source tracing showed that one fallback path preserves the source descriptor's declared dimension when resource creation fails. That confirms part of the reproduction path, but not the original logical cause: the title descriptor, heap index mapping, stale slot, or shader expectation may be wrong. Do not “fix” this by changing every null descriptor to Tex
### 4. D3D12 state and memory edge cases were fixed in focused changes
- [PR #5](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/pull/5): rate-limits repetitive high-water descriptor warnings. This reduces log noise; it does not solve high-index descriptor mapping.
- [PR #6](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/pull/6): fixes dynamic descriptor allocation when a free contiguous range crosses the search cursor. Includes exhaustive small-heap comparison tests.
- [PR #9](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/pull/9): makes zero-length title-memory writes/remaps true no-ops, avoiding accidental page dirtiness or alias-link removal from unaligned empty ranges.

- [PR #12](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/pull/12): adds opt-in handling for group barriers identified as divergent or potentially cut short. It retains memory/UAV fences and changes only the group wait. It is an experiment, not proof that barriers caused the observed TDR; the default behavior remains unchanged.

- [PR #13](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/pull/13) and [PR #14](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/pull/14): restore/rebind descriptor heaps and the appropriate root signature after internal depth-twin work and root-signature switches.
- [PR #15](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/pull/15): adds bounded diagnostics for concrete descriptor-heap pointers and root-signature bindings.

The active PR #16 branch contains a non-destructive indirect-argument clamp redesign. The earlier helper modified the title's argument shadow in place and did not use the optional count buffer when deciding which records to process. The branch implementation instead reads source arguments and count as SRVs, processes at most min(max, count), writes active records into reusable device-local scratch, and has ExecuteIndirect consume that scratch. It also uses bounded/saturating work-budget accounti

Tests cover source immutability, count-limited output, untouched tail sentinels, scratch/budget state across command-list replay, and GPU/WARP paths where available. Do not start clamp-hoisting or aggressive batching until this scratch/count behavior is stable and measured on the real target workload.
- Query resource-allocation information from the live host texture description rather than the guest/title description, following [VIctory PR #2286](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory/pull/2286).
- Give pipeline compiler worker threads a larger stack (64 MiB), following the NVIDIA driver stack-overflow investigation in [VIctory issue #966](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory/issues/966).

- **ztrx:** pipeline-wait controls and Wave64/group-barrier changes are useful comparison points, but reported frame-time and memory results are workload-specific. One lane-mask optimization was later reverted; do not port an intermediate revision without understanding its regression.

- **VIctory:** the live-host-texture allocation-info fix and larger pipeline-worker stack address concrete D3D12/NVIDIA failure classes. R4Y's feature branch ports the underlying ideas, not the entire fork.

- **victory-fork:** descriptor-state invalidation, view lookup, memory tracking, copy-back, and texture-streaming changes are relevant leads. A broad multi-subsystem PR should not be copied as one patch.

- **XCL:** its reports around the exact title watchdog offset and Wave64/TDR behavior are the closest external diagnostic comparison. Its reports suggest that more than one split-Wave64 compute shader may matter; disabling a single shader can stop one observed hang without resolving all hangs. Its translator and runtime differ from R4Y's, so hashes and fixes are not directly interchangeable.

A supplemental audit of [Belobug/VIctory-Belobug-AMD](https://github.com/Belobug/VIctory-Belobug-AMD) is recorded in [VICTORY_AMD_FORK_AUDIT.md](https://github.com/cmyk-ux/r4y/blob/feature/wave64-host-target/.agent/VICTORY_AMD_FORK_AUDIT.md). The fork's README reports world rendering on one RX 9070 XT but not playability; its FPS, workarounds, and AMD-specific shader behavior are self-reported and were not independently reproduced on R4Y's RTX 3070. The most transferable research candidates are
1. Record the exact repository URL, branch, HEAD SHA, OS, adapter/driver, title build, runtime profile, cache state, and timestamp. Do not combine logs from different builds or runs.

4. Keep the following failure categories separate: unsupported Wave64 translation, pipeline creation failure, long GPU dispatch, D3D12 device removal/TDR, descriptor type/index mismatch, title watchdog exception, and memory/allocator failure.

6. When inspecting a title crash, treat T: as a virtual title filesystem mount, not necessarily a host drive. With the default data root, title temp data is under %LOCALAPPDATA%\R4Y\data\7952987A\temp and R4Y's own exception log is a sibling crashes.log; honor any R4Y_DATA_DIR or configured data path override.

The rational stopping point is to preserve the repository, complete the exact-head review/CI for PR #16, retain the RTX 3070 test evidence and diagnostic artifacts, and stop expanding general features until the GPU-progress failure and descriptor mapping limitations have a defensible explanation or a narrow reproducible fix. Keep the project available for future research; do not confuse pausing product expansion with discarding the findings.

daeken/XSXEmu: README

An experimental Rust emulator for Xbox Series X|S AMD64 titles on Apple Silicon. XSXEmu runs guest CPU code through Rosetta in an x86-64 Mach-O process and develops native Xbox shader translation to Metal separately. It does not use Wine. Inspection, static linking, and non-executable mapping are portable. No game is playable yet, and guest execution is **not sandboxed**.

README

- **Shader translation:** Rust lifts a bounded subset of native GFX10 instructions and generates MSL. Owned tests on Apple M4 cover compute, graphics exports, and vertex-to-pixel interpolation. The reusable vertex/pixel translator requires explicit bindings; an owned interpolated pair has been baked offline and replayed from a strict Metal binary archive in a fresh process, matching **64/64 reference pixels**. Changing the interpolation channel changes the pixels and causes a strict archive miss
README

- **Shipped pipelines:** The preflight accounts for **28,164 rows in the pinned pipeline library; 0 are verified ready to bake**. Static audits can find closed control-flow graphs, but that does not establish the runtime-selected shader body, entry point, or bindings. README

On Apple Silicon under Rosetta, `run <trusted-fixture.exe> --experimental-static-tls` starts a time-bounded child process for the initial thread's static TLS. Adding `--rust-providers` in this lane permits only explicitly audited Win32 provider signatures. Other providers are refused unless tracing is enabled, in which case their slots also get diagnostic thunks. Combining `--experimental-static-tls` and `--trace-missing-imports` opts into treating every traced slot as callable; PE import metada
README

The Rust FLS provider implements `FlsAlloc`, `FlsGetValue`, `FlsSetValue`, and `FlsFree` with 127 process-wide indices and separate values for each guest thread’s implicit fiber. FLS is separate from dynamic and static TLS. Callback registration does not invoke guest code. If `FlsFree`, worker exit, or launcher teardown would need to invoke a registered callback for a non-null value, execution stops with a diagnostic instead. Fiber creation and switching are not supported.
README

With `--rust-providers`, `LoadLibraryExW` and `FreeLibrary` can acquire and release references to startup-mapped guest DLLs on the startup thread. `LoadLibraryExW` takes a bare case-insensitive DLL name (default `.dll` extension) and a null file handle. Flags `0` select the first mapped DLL with that name; `LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32` (`0x800`) limits matches to DLLs already registered as direct children of guest `C:\Windows\System32`. Paths and other flags are unsupported. Neither mode opens
README

The experimental static-TLS lane provides a limited guest TEB; full Windows exception dispatch, dynamic mapping of new libraries, and live Xbox graphics are not implemented. Static AMD64 unwind primitives do not provide exception dispatch. Don't substitute desktop D3D12 for `d3d12_xs.dll`: the Xbox device, memory, and layout contracts need an explicit adapter.

edupode/anyxboxseries: See [Build on Windows](docs/BUILD.md) to compile or contribute changes. The [shader tools](docs/SHADERS.md) require Python for container preparation and Microsoft's DXC for runtime HLSL compilation.

The Direct3D 12 shader probe checks SM 6.6 compute and DXR 1.1 inline ray tracing. The preparation tool can inspect DXBC/DXIL, unpack FSSM, and lift a subset of RDNA 2 scalar instructions into HLSL for the compute probe.

In viewer/source, Launcher.cs runs the resource viewer and PackageReader.cs reads MicrosoftGame.Config, the package manifest, and the layout files. It checks which files are present, looks for PE entry points, and opens the PNGs in the selected folder. The build.ps1 script compiles the viewer with the .NET Framework compiler.
`inspect_ui_resources.py` indexes RBF0 schema roots in readable zlib streams in local RPF9 archives. It reports stream offsets and aggregate schema counts without writing archive data.

The Direct3D bridge is implemented in d3d12_xs.cpp, with its exports declared in d3d12_xs.def. It forwards two root signature functions to the Windows runtime and records the result in shim_log.txt. fablinoo/kelvaroq: Kelvaroq is an Xbox Series X|S compatibility runtime for Windows x64, written in Rust. Its native engine is built on VIctory and victory-fork. The goal is a playable scene at 3840×2160 and 30 rendered fps, with correct textures and steady frame pacing on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

> **Ranked #1 of 44 projects** on an independent public tracker of PC compatibility efforts for this console title (check of 25 November 2026, 21:02 UTC): furthest along, two steps short of its "playable" bar of 20 fps and 30 minutes without a crash.

A console game is native x64 code: it runs on a PC processor as it is. We measured it. With nothing drawn, the game's own code holds a locked **30 fps** in its heaviest prologue scene on our test PC (5,331 heavy frames, 99th percentile 33.9 ms). Draw the same scene through a compatibility layer and it takes about **130 ms** a frame.

Those extra 100 ms are not the game, and they are not the GPU, which sits idle most of the frame. About two thirds of them go to keeping two copies of memory in sync, every frame: watch the pages, copy what changed up to the GPU, copy what the GPU wrote back. The Xbox has one memory. A PC has two.

Every public project we have measured on the same machine is built on that copy loop, and most of them keep iterating on it: AI-generated switch sets, more threads, one more patch to the copy path. Each pass moves a few milliseconds, breaks something else, and the open world still runs at 2 to 12 fps. A loop that should not exist cannot be tuned away.

We traced how the game really uses its memory, from the first instruction of the process to the open world, and found why the earlier attempts to remove the loop failed. The blocker was never the game.

**Kelvaroq's memory layer is in testing now, and the first results are wild:** in the first scenes we tested, the memory copied every frame fell from over 100 MB to under 8 MB. We are tuning it for the open world before it ships.

- **Goal:** the game runs from boot to credits exactly as it does on an Xbox Series X, with what a PC adds on top: DLSS super resolution, frame generation, higher resolutions and an unlocked frame rate.

- **Release policy:** the next public engine changes will land once the memory layer is validated across the whole game, DLSS and frame generation are integrated, the remaining visual effects are in place, and every test suite passes. Until then, the public build stays on the current engine while the new layer is tested.

**The prologue is playable at about 10 rendered fps in typical views and 7 to 8 fps in its heaviest scenes.** All measurements below are from the prologue at 3840×2160 on an RTX 5080. A heavy frame is a present with at least 3,000 draws.
Verified in play: the menus work, the character can be controlled, the HUD is shown, the game pauses, and sessions have run without a crash.

Patches 0041–0042 cut median heavy-frame time from 198.3 to 119.8 ms, and patches 0044–0048 to 108.5 ms. The thread that prepares and submits GPU work now limits heavy frames: the GPU waits for it. About 7% of draws are still dropped, mostly because ray-tracing structures are not built yet. Textures wait for space when VRAM is full.

The before and after runs used the same save and the same warm pipeline cache for 300 s each. Captures from both runs were checked for rendering errors. Frame times and mean fps in the table cover heavy frames. - **0 to 9 min, loading:** fps swung between about 1 and 20, with six samples at 4 fps or less. The last dip came at 8 min 45 s.
- **After 10 min:** fps stayed between about 9 and 12, with no further marked dip, for the remaining 26 min 46 s.
- **RAM:** a 15.5 GB peak at the start, then about 10.5 GB until 33 min, then about 7 GB until the end. Memory did not keep rising during this session, although one session cannot rule out a leak.

**Tester's verdict:** stable for 36 minutes, about 10 fps overall and 11 fps after loading, still far from smooth. An overall CPU use of about 15 % does not locate the bottleneck. A single saturated thread, the GPU or render synchronisation could each be the limit. Our own measurements, described above and in the documentation, point to the thread that prepares and submits GPU work.
- [x] Pin victory-fork to `f85101b` and apply patches 0001–0037 for texture uploads and placement, parallel refresh and pipeline waits, among other changes.

- [x] Apply patches 0038–0040 to read table constants from the GPU copy, place read-only copies in CPU-visible VRAM through Resizable BAR, submit work on a dedicated thread and run copies on the copy engine.

- [x] Apply patches 0041–0042 so the GPU launches mesh draws through an amplification stage, eliminating the clamp pass and full waits between mesh draws. GPU hashing uses 64 threads per block. Together these changes cut median heavy-frame time by 40%.
- [x] Copy game memory in place instead of through the kernel (patch 0044): 7–12% less frame time at 5,000 draws and more; frame-time spikes over one second are gone.
- [x] Present asynchronously, at most two frames ahead (patches 0046, 0048): the game no longer waits in present; p95 568 → 262 ms.
- [x] Shader preloading screen in the launcher, and a live performance monitor (`Kelvaroq.exe --monitor`).
- [ ] Remove the memory synchronisation that costs about two thirds of every heavy frame. *In testing: copies per frame down from over 100 MB to under 8 MB in the first scenes.*
- [ ] Address the VRAM budget and missing host pipelines.
- [ ] DLSS super resolution and frame generation on NVIDIA RTX GPUs.
- [ ] Reach 30 rendered fps in the heavy prologue scene, then the whole game from boot to credits.

`Kelvaroq.exe --experimental-render` (or `kelvaroq play --experimental-render <folder>`) starts an older experimental profile that reserves up to 256 MiB for VRAM transfers and 128 MiB for small read-only resources. It is not faster on the RTX 5080; the default settings are recommended. User-defined `VICTORY_*` settings take precedence. [Memory and submission settings](documentation.md#placement-mémoire-et-soumission)

Settings are stored in `%APPDATA%\Kelvaroq\settings` (schema 2). Storage moves create a dedicated child folder in the selected destination, verify its contents and switch the engine to the new location. Clearing shaders removes the translated shader directory. Clearing title data takes a recovery snapshot first.

The monitor starts disabled and attaches to the launched engine's process ID when selected. `VICTORY_LAUNCHER_MONITOR=0` suppresses it. Shader preload starts enabled and honours the existing `VICTORY_PIPELINE_PRECOMPILE=0` override. The desktop form uses the .NET Framework 4.8 WPF assemblies supplied by Windows. The package ships the desktop companion alongside the Rust entry point.

The workspace shows the high-performance hardware adapter, its driver and dedicated VRAM, the CPU and its physical and logical core counts, RAM, and the Windows build. It checks feature level 12.0, Shader Model 6.6, mesh shaders, resource binding tier 3 and root signature 1.1. The engine builds directly indexed descriptor heaps. Settings also reports wave widths, enhanced barriers and GPU upload heap support. On discrete GPUs the upload heap query reports whether the engine can use CPU-visible V

Automatic uses the following limits for the preferred compatible discrete GPU. The memory classes use total physical memory reported by Windows, rounded to the nearest GiB. Texture residency continues to follow the current DXGI budget, and the engine already trims idle pipeline library pages according to available RAM.
| Engine setting | Smaller configurations | At least 10 GiB VRAM and 16 GiB RAM | At least 16 GiB VRAM and 32 GiB RAM |

On multi-GPU PCs the launcher profiles the preferred discrete device. Windows selects the adapter for each executable. Select **High performance** for `kelvaroq-engine.exe` in Windows Graphics settings to use that device. The engine checks the active adapter's wave width again before pairing. An unsupported or unverified graphics requirement leaves the engine settings at their inherited values.

The native build script fetches the pinned revision, applies the rendering patches and adds `native/kelvaroq-render` to the build. To use an existing clone, run `python scripts/build_native.py --source <clone>`. The native engine can use VIctory's local saves and cache.

`inspect` reports a PE file's hash, entry point, sections and imports. With `--json`, it also reports the addresses needed for startup. `boot` executes instructions in guest memory. Replace the example path with the path to your local file.

The reference check builds two pinned revisions of the GFX10 translator, runs the programs on the named hardware adapter and compares the values read back. It covers eight sign-extension cases and two programs that select different textures per lane. On the development RTX 5080, all eight integer results and all 64 texture samples matched.

Git and Cargo are required. The first run fetches the revisions and caches the Git objects under `target/shader-reference/`. The `--source` option accepts a local clone containing both commits. The check validates the external translator on controlled programs. During native execution, the backend also translates shaders when it creates pipelines.

Kelvaroq is free software under the GPL-3.0-or-later, and that licence allows forks. It does not cover the **Kelvaroq name and logo**: a fork or a redistributed build must not use them, nor present itself as an official Kelvaroq release. Official builds come only from this repository and from Stellarr Studio SAS.

focusran/PS5-EMULATOR-PORT-GTA6: **PS5 Next-Gen Emulator** is an open-source, low-overhead virtualization and syscall translation environment designed to run PlayStation 5 titles natively on modern x86-64 PC hardware. This specialized branch focuses on shader pipeline optimization, custom I/O decompression, and memory management tailored for **Grand Theft Auto VI**.
* **🎨 RDNA 2 to Vulkan / DX12 Translation:** Real-time SPIR-V shader recompilation with asynchronous pipeline caching to eliminate stuttering.
* **🧠 Unified Memory Emulation:** Dynamic RAM/VRAM allocation bridge replicating the 16GB GDDR6 unified memory architecture.
* **⚡ Unlocked Framerates:** Built-in frame-pacing patches supporting 60+ FPS and ultrawide resolutions (21:9 / 32:9).
fqwfqwfqfa/GTA-6-PC-Version-Port-Reverse: It collects the console build analysis, the RAGE engine file formats, and the AI emulation layer that translates the original instruction and memory model into something a Windows x64 machine can execute — one launch chain instead of a folder of loose tools. Whether you want to unpack the archives, inspect the shader pipeline, or just boot the game and walk around Vice City, this package covers the path.

The layer runs externally and reads the game image from your own legal copy, so the base install is never permanently modified. The package includes a low-latency debug overlay with full instrumentation.
| **Asset Pipeline** | Archive unpack, texture conversion, and shader translation. |
| **AI Emulation Layer** | Instruction mapping, memory translation, and frame pacing. |

A: The layer operates externally and does not alter the game image on disk. It does, however, execute translated code, so a mismatch between your game build and the layer build is the most common crash source.

hedge-dev/XenonRecomp: The instruction implementations operate on little-endian values. However, since the Xbox 360 is a big-endian machine, the memory load instructions swap endianness when reading values, and memory store instructions reverse it to big-endian before writing. All the memory loads and stores are marked volatile to prevent Clang from doing unsafe code reordering.

Virtual function calls are resolved by creating a "perfect hash table" at runtime, where dereferencing a 64-bit pointer (using the original instruction address multiplied by 2) gives the address of the recompiled function. This was previously implemented by creating an 8 GB virtual allocation, but it had too much memory pressure. Now it relies on function addresses being placed after the valid XEX memory region in the base memory pointer. These regions are exported as macros in the output `ppc_c

Each frame, GR2port takes the game's scene at the start of its frame graph and draws it on its own render thread, so it never builds or translates per-draw PS4 GPU commands. **The CPU overhead of the native renderer was measured as only 0.8ms in frame time**.

**As a disclaimer, this port does not rewrite the entire source code of the game (just the graphics source code). Since the game's executable already contains x86-64 code, a developmental shortcut was made to natively execute the code in the game's executable directly.  It does, however, port the graphics by reverse engineering each graphical pass and rewriting them natively for Vulkan** (this is not static recompilation). The original game logic is patched via a runtime memory patcher for PC en

**All shader pipelines are precompiled** at boot and stored on disk so there is no shader stutter during gameplay. A runtime translates the firmware libraries the game calls on the PS4's operating system into native PC operating system solutions (little to no performance overhead like WINE).

kellysix/kelly: Kelly is an experimental fork of VIctory, a compatibility layer that runs an Xbox Series X|S title natively on Windows using files you supply. It follows upstream `main` and focuses on getting the world to render correctly and improving performance on the test PC.

VIctory by Marvisak and its contributors is the base of everything here: the loader, the runtime services, the Direct3D 12 back end and the shader recompiler. Licensed GPL-3.0-or-later; so is this fork. Upstream's history is kept intact below the single commit that carries this fork's changes.

The guard over every view of a memory page is code by myokex (victory-amd, commit c6dc4d8), which adapts pull request #115 here by Spexivus, its correction by joroyt and a part of VIctory #1122 by tightfall. The read-beside fix for kernel reads into title memory is by Joshua Odom (commit 10ea38e of the same fork family). Both are carried here unchanged apart from one merge conflict.

Kelly can boot the title, play the opening cutscene and reach the prologue. Gameplay remains experimental because of low frame rates and rendering issues. All Kelly results below come from one Windows 11 PC with an Intel Core i7-14700KF, an NVIDIA RTX 4070 with 12 GB of VRAM, and 32 GB of RAM. Tests used the Series X profile.
| Boot, menus and start screen | Work at the title's 30 fps. |
| Performance | Early world tests ran at roughly 2.5–4 fps. Later first-room tests reached about 4.5–5 fps with defaults, with higher results under experimental settings. |
| Stability | Normal runs stayed up on the test PC after a wave64 barrier regression was fixed. Experimental draw windows have caused device loss. |
- Corrected the buffer view used by meshlet culling so world geometry can draw.
- Fixed per-draw descriptor table exhaustion that could send draws to unallocated slots and hang the GPU.
- Fixed readback of compute-generated lighting data for sky, probes and fog across mip levels and layers.
- Fixed gathers that read mip level zero when the shader requested another level, including gathers with offsets.
- Added support for rectangle lists, paired depth and stencil views for compute-written depth textures, and texture readbacks.

- Ray tracing is experimental and off by default. The title's acceleration-structure builder shaders translate, shaders can read title memory by raw address, and the ray-box and ray-triangle tests are emulated in DXIL and checked against a GPU reference. At the recorded checkpoint, 59 of 64 trace programs translated. See [the ray-tracing notes](docs/fork-ray-tracing.md).

- Descriptor records copied directly by the title are mirrored before submission. Pull request #305 by Flyander, after upstream VIctory `86a5ed6`, covered about 40,000 records per frame whose host slots had been empty or stale.

- Reserving VRAM for first-frame render targets and buffers allowed 98 buffer copies totalling 945 MB, compared with one copy in earlier runs. CPU-side comparison for shader writes fell from 550–710 MB per frame to about 25 MB.

- An early on-demand mip test used the software adapter. A later hardware run with fixes from pull request #747 by AscilCH avoided allocating about 3.1 GB for mip levels the title did not hold and completed without device loss. Enable it with `VICTORY_LEVELS_ON_DEMAND=1`. It is off by default.

- Opening guarded blocks for storage writes became the default in the later update. Fourteen more shader programs translated. The first-half interpolation fallback is applied only after a related translation failure because applying it globally changed 8,551 working pixel programs.
- A copy between title textures backed by the same host texture is skipped. A five-minute run saw 402 such copies.
- Memory-value waits, write-watch queries and page queries avoid walking page tables on each call.

- Kernel reads use a temporary buffer before copying into title memory so a block guarded again during the read can still receive the data. Failed page-destination reads are retried. Set `VICTORY_DSTORAGE_RETRIES=0` for the previous behavior.

- Large title buffers can have GPU-resident copies, with GPU hashing used to find shader writes. `VICTORY_INPLACE=1` enables experimental use of title memory as a graphics heap. The first stage was verified with a probe on the test GPU.

- The test card used 85–99% of its VRAM budget during world runs. A five-minute run released about 26,000 texture copies and recreated about 3,400. Active render targets used roughly 2.8 GB. Rejected texture slots are deferred briefly so the sweep can reach other slots. `VICTORY_FULL_CARD_PASS=0` restores earlier sweep behavior. `VICTORY_CARD_ROOM_FOR_BUFFERS=1` enables an optional buffer reservation.

- The bindless texture queue skips stale views, the view table is bounded, and the pipeline library is memory-mapped. A fix prevents replacement of the library file while it is mapped, which had caused intermittent device loss.

- Shader cleanup includes dead-code elimination, constant folding and value reuse. It cut host instructions in the shader pack by about 43% and saved about 20 ms of GPU time per frame on the test PC. `VICTORY_SHADER_OPT=0` disables it.

- The first rendering update put the first room at 190–450 ms per frame. Descriptor fingerprinting and leaving draw-table slots to their draws reduced the heap pass from 70–220 ms to about 3 ms per frame. A reader-writer lock and per-page updates also reduced contention. Guarded memory was excluded from write-watch queries following work by Jonirulah in #670 and follow-up work after triippywhale.
- A later first-room session reached 6–7 fps with the settings below enabled together. Defaults measured about 4.5–5 fps in that session.

- Subsequent profiling measured a typical 136 ms frame with windows off. The render thread waited 77 ms inside present, while the submit thread spent 118 ms on work including 41 ms copying title memory and 40 ms on copy-back. GPU utilization was 85–98%. Of roughly 130 ms of GPU work, about 16 ms updated GPU copies, 10 ms ran comparisons, and 102 ms went to the title's lists with per-record clamping. Total frame time tracked draw count at around 32 µs per draw.
- In that later session, draw windows raised average first-room performance from 6.0 to 8.9 fps and opening-cutscene performance from 3.1 to 4.2 fps. Results depend on the scene, build and switches.
| `VICTORY_ASYNC_SUBMIT=1` | Moves submission preparation and dispatch to a worker. One profile had the title's render thread inside submission for 257 of 292 ms per frame. |

| `VICTORY_QUEUE2=1` | Moves fetches of shader writes to a copy queue. The copy-back thread's wait fell from around 125 ms to 7 ms per frame. Includes a fix for fetches next to a later in-flight submission. |
| `VICTORY_TEXTURE_NO_WAIT=1` | Allows texture refreshes during memory remapping. Loading samples above one second fell from 18 to 5. |
| `VICTORY_MERGE_GAP=64 VICTORY_MERGE_RUNS=4096` | Merges small gaps between title writes under in-flight shader writes. The merge is approximate. See the source comment at `merge_gap`. |

Upload fills and read-only buffer copies proceed without waiting by default and are checked against subsequent writes. No mismatch was recorded in the reported runs. `VICTORY_FILL_WAIT=1` restores the wait. Up to 512 idle host lists and texture staging buffers are reused.

Other switches built and unit-tested include `VICTORY_COPY_PLAIN=1`, `VICTORY_REFRESH_ONCE=1`, `VICTORY_VIEW_KNOWN=1`, `VICTORY_BACK_OWN_VIEW=1` and `VICTORY_ASYNC_PRESENT=1`. Their benefit remains unverified. `VICTORY_BVH_HOLD=1` stays off because testing showed a loss of indirect light. `VICTORY_EFFICIENCY_MODE=1` keeps the system's efficiency policy in effect. In one hybrid-CPU run, the title's render and recording threads were sampled on fast cores throughout, and the submit worker was sampl
- `VICTORY_WAVE_WIDE=1` enables the 64-lane barrier form that caused a hang in testing. It is off by default.
- Gameplay used around 24 GB of memory. The indirect per-record clamp and transfers between system memory and VRAM remain major costs.
- A Direct3D 12 GPU with Shader Model 6.6. The world requires mesh shader support.

kfedora/GTAVI-Xbox2PC: **An open-specification static recompilation pipeline, DXIL-to-SPIR-V shader translator, and Xbox Era OS shim architecture for executing the Grand Theft Auto VI console binary natively on x86_64 PCs.**

> **`kfedora/GTAVI-Xbox2PC` hosts ZERO copyrighted assets, ZERO console executables, ZERO decryption keys, and ZERO source code.** This public repository serves strictly as the **architectural specification, compatibility ledger, and community benchmark hub**.

Unlike traditional hypervisor or HLE/LLE console emulators that suffer massive dynamic recompilation (JIT) overhead at runtime, this architecture statically lifts the leaked Xbox Series X|S executable (`Leonida_Retail_XSX.xex` / PE32+ container) into native Windows and Linux `x86_64-v3` object code via LLVM 21, while intercepting Xbox Era kernel syscalls and RAGE9 engine memory barriers at near-zero CPU instruction penalty.
* **Shader & Material Pipeline:** Real-time translation of Xbox DXIL Shader Model 6.7 bytecode into host DX12 and Vulkan 1.4 SPIR-V.
* **Texture Streaming & Geometry:** Hardware BC7/BCn texture pass-through, skeletal animation, and Euphoria physics integration.
* **Interactive Gameplay Milestones:** Multiple private builds have completed **Lucia's Prologue** end-to-end and entered **Jason's opening mission (*"Gone Fishing"*)** at **1 to 5 FPS**.
|  • Replaces custom Jaguar/Zen2 cache-line prefetches & Xbox-only intrinsics      |
|  >>> OUTPUT: Lucia walking around the prologue at a majestic 2.4 FPS <<<         |

One of the primary engineering challenges in bringing an Xbox Series X binary to PC is the **Unified Memory Architecture (UMA)**. The console shares a single **16 GB GDDR6** pool (10 GB high-bandwidth `560 GB/s` + 6 GB lower-bandwidth `336 GB/s`, with ~13.5 GB accessible to games) directly between CPU and GPU without PCIe transfers.
On standard x86_64 PCs with discrete GPUs, `GTAVI-Xbox2PC` enforces a split-mirror virtual memory bridge:
| `0x0000_1000_0000` – `0x0002_8000_0000` | 10.0 GB | High-Speed GPU/CPU | Pinned `DEVICE_LOCAL \| HOST_VISIBLE` (ReBAR) | Exhausts 12GB/16GB VRAM cards immediately |
| `0x7FFE_0000_0000` – `0x7FFF_FFFF_FFFF` | Dynamic | TLS & Stack | Remapped to Host `std::jthread` Stack | Thread #7 decompression stack overflow |

> **Resizable BAR (ReBAR) / Smart Access Memory is mandatory.** Disabling ReBAR in your motherboard UEFI reduces prologue performance from **2.4 FPS** down to **0.18 FPS** (roughly 1 frame every 5.5 seconds) due to constant 256MB staging aperture flushes.

People frequently ask why an **RTX 5070 Ti** paired with a **Ryzen 7 7800X3D** renders the prologue at just **1–3 FPS** while GPU utilization hovers around **18%**. Below is an actual captured `416.6 ms` frame budget (~2.4 FPS) from a private build trace:

**Key Takeaway:** The GPU itself finishes drawing a frame of *Grand Theft Auto VI* in **~14.5 ms** (roughly 69 FPS capable). The remaining **402.1 ms** is pure CPU-side synchronization, memory copying, and shader translation overhead. Once asynchronous pipeline caching and dirty-page tracking replace full-frame memory flushes, frame rates are projected to jump significantly.

1. My RTX 5070 Ti is only getting 2.4 FPS! Is my GPU broken?

No. Your GPU is barely doing anything (~18% usage). Nearly 96% of your frame time is currently spent waiting on synchronous shader translation and uncached CPU-to-GPU memory barrier copies. Treat it as a playable slideshow of the future.

If you enabled debug logging or intermediate DXIL caching, the translation pipeline writes uncompressed shader IR and pipeline state objects to disk on every draw-call cache miss. Unlike certain recent GPU driver bugs, this excessive SSD write behavior is entirely our fault.

The RAGE9 water buoyancy solver experiences a floating-point division singularity whenever frame time exceeds `333 ms` (below 3 FPS). Look straight down at the wooden planks of the dock to cull ocean reflections until your framerate climbs above 3.5 FPS, then proceed with the cutscene.

The compute shader responsible for wind-swaying foliage vertex buffers uses an Xbox-specific `WavePrefixSum` intrinsic that hasn't been mapped in `vkd3d` yet, causing the material shader to fall back to the engine's missing-shader debug color.

**Proof the output is identical:** the benchmark prints a checksum of every scan result, every decoded pixel and the whole search index. All of them match between v1.4.8 and v1.5.0, and a save then reload of the scan index gives back the same data. Full raw output: [`docs/bench/v1.4.8_vs_v1.5.0.txt`](docs/bench/v1.4.8_vs_v1.5.0.txt).
**Run it yourself:** `PercyStar.exe --bench "<game folder>" [runs] [filter]` (filter is a comma list such as `cache,txd,data.rpf`).
- **BC1 / BC2 / BC3 / BC4 / BC5 / BC6H / BC7 decoding uses every CPU core** (image split into bands of block rows). BC7 was 80% of texture dictionary load time.
- **zlib now uses the `zlib-rs` backend** (pure Rust, faster inflate) for all archive reads.

- **Archive scanning probes every 4 KB page on all cores** and reads the next 16 MB chunk on its own thread while the current one is probed, so the disk never waits. Same for the levels.rpf vehicle index.

rpatty-dev/turbine: Turbine is a userscript for playing **GTA VI over Xbox Remote Play in the browser** (`play.xbox.com`). It turns your keyboard and mouse into a virtual Xbox controller with GTA-style controls, mouse look and a car mode. It also adds a GPU upscaler, frame generation that doubles a 30 fps stream to 60 fps, and low-latency stream settings.
It doesn't modify the Xbox site's code. It adds a virtual controller through the browser's Gamepad API and draws the stream through its own WebGL layer, so site updates are less likely to break it.
- **Low-latency stream:** shrinks the WebRTC receive buffer (`jitterBufferTarget`). Set `JITTER_BUFFER_MS` to `30` if the stream stutters on weak Wi-Fi.
- **Upscaler:** draws the stream at your screen's native resolution on the GPU and sharpens it with AMD FidelityFX CAS (contrast adaptive sharpening). Adjust with `UPSCALE_SHARPNESS`.

- **Frame generation:** estimates motion between stream frames on the GPU and draws warped in-between frames. It turns on only when your display refreshes faster than the stream: a 30 fps stream on a 60 Hz screen becomes 60 fps, and a 60 fps stream on a 120 Hz ProMotion screen becomes 120 fps.
- **Stats overlay:** shows resolution, fps, ping, buffer delay, decode time and packet loss, so you can see the effect of each setting.

To draw a frame between two real ones, Turbine has to wait for the second one. That adds about half a stream frame of delay: around 17 ms at 30 fps, 8 ms at 60 fps. Generated frames can show smearing around edges, HUD elements and fast motion. Turn it off with F7 for competitive play.
- **Game settings:** if GTA VI offers a performance or high-frame-rate graphics mode on your console, use it. A higher stream frame rate cuts input delay more than frame generation can.
- **Console:** in Xbox Settings → Devices & connections → Remote features, pick the lowest-latency quality option if your console offers one.

shrewbrewsh/OpenRPF9: - **Stream carving:** Scans aligned offsets for compressed payloads and inflates them via `DeflateStream`. Each valid stream is tagged as `text` or `binary` based on printable ASCII/UTF-8 bytes.

- **Offset jumping:** Once a stream inflates, the scanner jumps past the consumed compressed bytes (`ms.Position`) and aligns to the next 16-byte boundary so it doesn't pick up false-positive fragments mid-stream.

In early community Mac experiments, frame counters often reported a steady "30 FPS", leading to assumptions that gameplay was already functioning smoothly. Rigorous telemetry and automated frame-dump analysis on an Apple Silicon M5 Pro revealed the underlying reality:
| Metric (120 s benchmark) | Baseline Port (`db065d8`) | Consolidated `mac-native` (`ee3c780` + patches) |

1. **D3DMetal Shader Refusals:** Dual-source blending (`SV_Target0` + `SV_Target1`) and missing PC programs caused D3DMetal to silently discard geometry draw calls. The presentation loop kept presenting an identical 2D loading frame.
3. **Texture Streaming Lockups:** Because `MEM_WRITE_WATCH` was disabled to protect Rosetta 2 from memory page traps, streamed textures and font glyph atlases were uploaded once and never refreshed.
- **Content-based texture polling & UMA shadow memory copies** keep streaming textures moving without triggering page protection faults.
- **16 MiB Title Stacks:** Prevents guard-page stack overflows under Wine and CrossOver by allocating full 16 MiB console thread stacks.

- **COM Vtable Prefix Mirroring (`PREFIX = 16`):** D3DMetal retrieves internal Metal encoders at negative offsets (`ext - 16`). Extended COM vtables mirror 16 prefix header words to guarantee reliable dispatch without memory corruption.

- **Dual-Source Blending Stand-Ins:** Implements `SV_Target0` + `SV_Target1` stand-in pixel shaders (PR [#666](https://github.com/ivall/xcl/pull/666)), preventing D3DMetal pipeline creation rejections.

- **Command-List Creation:** Device slot 73 distinguishes shader-cache sessions by their explicit interface IDs. On Mac hosts, console-only command-list IDs are translated to the standard PC graphics command-list interface.
- **Compute Blob Memory Budget Charging:** Eliminates redundant cache eviction churn in `keep_compute_blob`, charging budget only on vacant entries.

- **UMA Video Memory Shadowing (`Uma::shadowed`):** Emulates console shared memory without requiring `OpenExistingHeapFromAddress` (unsupported by Wine), enabling high-speed zero-copy CPU-to-GPU data flow.
- **Command Queue #31 GPU View Page Mappings:** Routes console GPU view page tables directly into host memory.

- **Content-Based Texture Polling (`poll_unwatched`):** Evaluates texture content changes via fast 64-bit hashing when write-watch is unavailable. Uploads skip textures while their host resources are being released.
- **Unchanged Texture Upload Skip (`XCL_TEXTURE_SKIP_UNCHANGED=1`):** Skips redundant GPU buffer re-uploads, saving precious PCIe/UMA bandwidth.
- **Isolated DXC Thread Heaps (`own_heaps`):** Allocates private heap spaces for parallel DXC shader compilation threads, eliminating concurrency crashes in Wine's memory manager.
| **Minecraft Preview** | `Microsoft.MinecraftBeta` 1.18.3064.0 | ✅ | Fully playable | 60+ FPS, world generation, audio, gamepad |
| `XCL_TEXTURE_SKIP_UNCHANGED` | `1` | `0` | Re-presents textures without re-uploading unchanged memory |

w1spo/xclayer: The fork focuses on stability, memory management, shader translation and runtime performance. Compatibility remains experimental; support varies by title, GPU and driver.
| Graphics | Direct3D 12 GPU with Shader Model 6.6 and mesh shader support |
| Shader compiler | DXC 1.8 or newer recommended |
| Memory | Sufficient RAM, disk space and system-managed page file for the title |

AMD RDNA hardware is the primary development target upstream. NVIDIA GPUs use a Wave64-to-Wave32 translation path where applicable, which can affect performance and correctness. Hardware support does not guarantee game compatibility.
- [DirectX Shader Compiler](https://github.com/microsoft/DirectXShaderCompiler/releases) (if the Windows SDK does not provide a suitable DXC version).

On Windows 10, the [Direct3D 12 Agility SDK](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/directx/directx12agility/) is required for Shader Model 6.6. Place the compatible `D3D12Core.dll` in a `D3D12` directory alongside `xcl.exe`, or set `XCL_D3D12_DIR` to the directory containing it. Include the matching SDK layers DLL if enabling the D3D12 debug layer.
The original game directory remains unchanged. Saves, configuration, shader caches and other writable data are stored separately.
- RDNA2 shader recompilation, asynchronous pipeline compilation and persistent shader caching.
- Direct3D 12 graphics and compute translation, texture detiling and GPU memory management.
- BCPack decoding for BC1, BC3, BC4, BC5, BC6H and BC7 streams; BC2 and hardware swizzle options remain unsupported.
- Diagnostic tooling for memory allocation, resource lifetime, streaming and graphics errors.
If startup fails, check the DXC version, GPU capabilities, Gaming Services and available system commit. The runtime's 24 GiB commit-headroom warning is advisory, not a fixed RAM requirement.

weile10000/xc2-ns2-recomp: > Release packages ship only the open-source launcher, generic runtime (`xc2_rt.dll`), and build toolchain. Game-derived builds (`xc2_boot.exe`, lifted game code) and translated shader caches (`.spv`) are never distributed — they are built locally on your own PC from your own legally acquired copy of the game.

3. **Play** — Click **Play**. On the very first boot per GPU driver, Vulkan compiles its pipeline cache briefly before entering the title screen.

| **Upscaler DLLs** *(optional)* | TAAU works out of the box; for FSR 3/4 or DLSS, use **Launcher → Settings → Upscaler** to fetch official NVIDIA Streamline / AMD FidelityFX packages into `upscalers/` |

└──▶ Vulkan 1.3 Replay ──▶ SPIR-V Cache (offline harness + Ryujinx translator)

zortos293/Lichii: README

Lichii uses its own profile: `%APPDATA%\lichii` on Windows, and the `lichii` directories under `$XDG_DATA_HOME`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` on Linux and macOS. Without XDG overrides, these are `~/.local/share/lichii`, `~/.config/lichii` and `~/.cache/lichii`. An existing portable `user/` directory still takes priority and is not imported or changed by the wizard.
README

On the first non-portable GUI launch, Lichii offers to import Eden and other detected emulator profiles. Back up `%APPDATA%\eden` first on Windows, or the old data, config and cache directories on Unix, and close the source emulator. Choose **Keep Old Data** to copy without changing the source, then check your saves and relaunch. Existing destination data is retained in backup directories rather than merged. Move also retains a source backup until you remove it yourself; Link deliberately shares
README

Compatibility and performance vary by game, hardware and driver. Rendering errors, stutters and crashes remain possible. Passing automated tests does not establish that a game renders correctly, and this project makes no universal frame-rate guarantee.
README

Desktop reporting requires a build containing [PR #303](https://github.com/zortos293/Lichii/pull/303) and is not available in build 88. In builds that include it, play and stop a Switch 2 game, then right-click that game and choose **Submit compatibility report**. Only the latest session in the current Lichii process is eligible.
README

Do not upload game files, keys, firmware or private account information. Bug bundles, GPU traces, shader dumps, pipeline caches and crash dumps can also contain game data. Do not attach them to public reports; ask a maintainer for handling instructions before sharing them. Plain-text logs should be checked for sensitive information before posting.
README
Lichii is free and stays free. If you want to help, you can donate in crypto. Donations help pay for the AI tools and build machines used to develop this open-source project faster.

zsy-miao/victory-perf: A performance- and lighting-focused Windows compatibility layer for running Xbox Series X|S (Scarlett) GDK titles natively on PC, derived from [fxceless/victory-fork](https://github.com/fxceless/victory-fork) and [Marvisak/VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory).

The project combines a native x86-64 PE32+ loader, console HLE modules (`xgameruntime`, `kernelx`, `d3d12_xs`, GameInput), a `d3d12_xs` → host D3D12 graphics backend, and an RDNA2 (GFX10) → DXIL shader recompiler, with targeted CPU/GPU synchronization optimizations, ahead-of-time shader precompilation, lighting stand-ins for shadowed interiors, Series S overlay compositing, and keyboard/mouse support.
| Boot, intro, and menus | ✅ Working | Runs at 30 fps target with audio and input |

| Frame rate (Series S, 50% render scale) | 🟡 4.5–14+ fps | **14 fps (71 ms)** prison corridor, **11 fps (95 ms)** heist interior, **9 fps (115 ms)** cell; **4.5–6.5 fps** in heavy scenes (~10,000 draws/frame) — up from 2.5–4 fps baseline |
| Stability (`--console series-s`) | ✅ Stable in testing | Avoids AMD FFX FSR4 `DXGI_ERROR_INVALID_CALL` crash via `VICTORY_OWN_UPSCALER=1`; no screen flicker observed |

*Caveats:* All benchmark numbers above are self-reported on a single Ryzen 7 9800X3D + RTX 4070 SUPER setup using `--console series-s` with `VICTORY_OWN_UPSCALER=1` and `VICTORY_RENDER_SCALE=0.5`. Lighting stand-ins approximate missing bounce/shadow light rather than reproducing console ray tracing.

- **Scoped indirect clamp barriers (`VICTORY_CLAMP_SCOPED`, default on):** Replaces global full-GPU UAV drains around `ExecuteIndirect` argument clamps with resource-scoped UAV barriers on dedicated argument/count buffers and removes the redundant post-clamp global barrier.

- **Per-list UAV barrier deduplication (`VICTORY_BARRIER_MERGE`, default on):** Tracks `uav_pending` (including image stores) per `HostList` and skips redundant global UAV barriers across `barrier_groups` and clamp passes.

- **Expanded indirect clamp windows & light PSO restore:** Enables `VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW` by default, increases `VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW_MOST` from `64` to `4096`, and enables `VICTORY_CLAMP_LIGHT_RESTORE` by default so graphics root bindings survive clamp dispatches.

- **CPU stall & spike elimination (`crates/victory-gpu/src/host.rs`, `resource.rs`, `texture.rs`):** Removed O(N²) loops in `host.rs`, moved `heap_buffers` pruning/refresh to 1/16th incremental work per frame (removing ~142 ms periodic spikes), relaxed VRAM texture eviction (`EVICT_IDLE_FRAMES=120`), enabled parallel refresh flushes, and enabled overlapped texture refreshes / fast hashing (`VICTORY_TEXTURE_OVERLAP`, `VICTORY_FAST_HASH`, `VICTORY_KNOWN_WRITES`, all default on).

- **Ahead-of-time shader precompilation (`apps/victory/src/precompile.rs`, `crates/victory-gpu/src/precompile.rs`, `shader_cache.rs`):** Precompiles cached RDNA2 → DXIL shader pipelines ahead of runtime to cut first-use hitches.
- **Memory copy, ReBAR, and readback helpers:** `crates/victory-gpu/src/memcopy.rs`, `rebar.rs`, and `readback.rs`.
**Requirements:** Windows 10/11 x64, AVX2-capable CPU, Direct3D 12 GPU with Shader Model 6.6 + Mesh Shaders, and the Rust toolchain pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml`.
